canvas.getContext("webgl") and ("webgl2"): OpenGL ES 2 and 3 for pages, drawn on the GPU through wgpu, with shaders translated by a rewrite of GLSL ES in front of naga. A page that never asks pays nothing but the size of the code: the script is evaluated at the first getContext or the first read of an interface, the GPU process is started once a page has shown its first content (webgl.gpu_start_ahead; off: by the first context of the browser), and the program does not link d3d12.dll (wgpu loads it when it is asked to, in that process).

Checked: the Three.js examples (a crate, Littlest Tokyo, a Ferrari, shadow maps, particles, bloom, instancing), MapLibre GL JS on its own site, and a conformance set of ours (examples/jsweb/webgl.js, native/webgl/src/tests.rs). The webgl folder of web-platform-tests is in wpt/suites.txt.

#The layers

LayerFileWhat
the interfacesnative/js/odin/web_webgl.js, web_webgl.odinWeb IDL: objects, overloads, conversions; which object is whose. Calls become words in a command buffer.
the crossingapi/webgl.widl, src/page/bindings_webgl.odin, src/webglA context on its canvas's backing; command buffers, questions, frames.
the processnative/webgl: parent.rs (browser), child.rs (GPU process), ipc/Starts, watches and ends the GPU process; what crosses, checked on both sides.
the devicenative/webgl: host.rs, gl.rs, draw.rs, capture.rs, query.rs, formats.rs, ops.rsIn the GPU process, a thread with a wgpu device per context: OpenGL ES's state machine, all its rules and its errors.
the shadersnative/webgl/src/translate.rsGLSL ES to what naga reads, and what WebGL must know of a shader.

Calls are written to a buffer and sent at the end of the task, when the buffer is full, or when the page has to wait for something (getError, readPixels, getShaderParameter, getParameter). What the realm answers by itself (isContextLost, getContextAttributes, getShaderPrecisionFormat) crosses nothing. So a frame of a thousand draws is one host call; a getError per draw is a round trip to another process per draw, as in other browsers.

The numbers of operations and the layout of the stream are in native/webgl/src/ops.rs, the same as in web_webgl.js.

#Why this design

The toolkit draws with Direct3D 11 on Windows and wgpu-native on Linux, and neither can run a page's shaders. ANGLE is not available. So:

  • One backend for both systems: wgpu, on a device of its own (Vulkan on a real GPU and Direct3D 12 otherwise on Windows, Vulkan on Linux, software adapters where there is no GPU). Only Rust crates are added, built with the one Rust library of wren.exe.
  • A process of its own, a thread per context in it. The page's thread never compiles anything and never waits for the GPU except when a page asks for an answer, and then with a deadline. A panic, a device lost or a shader that takes for ever to compile loses a context; a crash in a driver or FXC, or a thread that cannot come back, loses every context and nothing else (the GPU process).
  • Frames by the CPU. A frame is copied to a staging buffer, then into the shared section of its canvas, then into the canvas's bitmap, then to the toolkit's texture: the path of a 2D canvas, slow in principle (about 2 ms a frame for 2 megapixels here) and free of any sharing of textures between two devices. A shared texture is the way to save that copy, later.

#What wgpu has not, and what stands for it

GLHere
state changes between drawsa cache of pipelines per program, by the state that makes them
writes between drawswhat the open encoder used is written through the encoder (buffers) or after a submit (textures)
uniformsa block per stage (std140) kept by the context, copied per draw into a ring with dynamic offsets
window coordinatesframebuffers hold their bottom row first: the vertex shader negates y, front faces swap; a canvas is flipped when shown, and textures rendered to read back as GL says
clip z from -w to wrewritten at the end of the vertex shader
gl_PointSize, gl_PointCoorda variant of the vertex shader draws each point as an instanced quad (made on the first draw of points)
triangle fans, line loops, byte indicesindices generated into the ring
vertex formats wgpu lacks, strides that are not multiples of 4converted once per buffer version
RGB, luminance, alpha, 16-bit packed texturesexpanded to RGBA on upload
incomplete texturesa fallback texture of opaque black
generateMipmap, scaled blits, clears with a mask or scissordrawn
transform feedbacka variant of the vertex stage stores its varyings in storage buffers, in a pass of its own (capture.rs)
occlusion queries of GL, which last across passesan occlusion slot per pass they cross, resolved at each submit; the result is any of them
a vertex attribute divisor above 1the values written out per instance

#Shaders

naga's GLSL front end reads Vulkan-flavoured GLSL 450: it has the type checker and the lowering, it does not read GLSL ES. After the preprocessor (pp-rs, naga's own), translate.rs rewrites the token stream: no expression is parsed, only declarations.

  • attributes and varyings get locations (decided at link: a shader is translated again then);
  • default uniforms go into a block per stage; structures, global constants and uniforms are hoisted above the code;
  • a sampler becomes a texture and a sampler, texture2D(map, uv) becomes texture(sampler2D(map_t, map_s), uv), and a sampler passed to a function two parameters. An array of samplers takes a constant index, as GLSL ES 1.00 and 3.00 require;
  • bool and matrices of two rows, which uniforms cannot hold, are held as uint and vec4 and copied to a private variable when main starts; matrices as attributes and varyings become their columns;
  • modf and matrixCompMult, which naga has not, are written into shaders that name them.

getActiveUniform and friends come from what was declared; offsets from naga's module. What naga does not check is not checked: implicit conversions from int to float compile, and the loop restrictions of GLSL ES 1.00 are not enforced.

#The GPU process

One per browser: the same executable, started with --wren-gpu-process=<handles>. (A package initializer of src/webgl looks at the arguments before main, so any program that links the browser can be one. It costs that look. Tests: src/tools/e2e/webgl_process.odin.) A process with no context left goes after webgl.gpu_idle_exit_s.

Made ahead. A page's thread waits for its getContext: for a process to start (about 200 ms on a desktop with a GPU) and for a device to be made in it (70 ms; a quarter of it the context's own shaders). So both are made before a page asks:

  • the browser starts the process when a page has shown its first content (webgl.gpu_start_ahead, on by default), on a thread of its own, with the attributes a context would have (wg_start_ahead): the page's thread never waits for it. Nothing when a process runs, or when one ended badly within webgl.gpu_restart_window_s: a restart is for a page that asks. A process started ahead that goes idle (webgl.gpu_idle_exit_s) without ever having had a context turns this off for the browser's life: a browser that sees no WebGL pays for one start, not one a minute. Off: the first context of the browser starts it, and a browser that sees no WebGL starts nothing;
  • the process holds the next context's device, made on a thread of its own (native/webgl/src/spare.rs, a state machine: empty, being made, ready): after its start (Prepare), and after each context that took one. A context waits for the one being made rather than make a second; one made for other preferences (webgl.force_software, webgl.backend) is dropped. Not on a software adapter, where devices are made in turns and a context's first messages would wait for one nobody may ask for.

What a page sees does not change: getContext still answers once its device exists, null when there is none, with the same attributes and extensions; getError, readPixels and getParameter are the device's answers as before. On npr.org a script asks for four contexts after the load event, two in OffscreenCanvas (one in a worker): 380 ms of the window thread before; after, not measured yet on a GPU (the round was finished on a Linux machine with a software adapter only) (round 60).

What crossesHow
commands, questions, answerstwo byte rings (16 MiB each way) in one section of shared memory; a message longer than a ring goes through in pieces as the reader takes them. A reader spins a little, then sleeps; a doorbell wakes it
framesa section per canvas with three pictures: the child fills one and swaps it with the one published, the browser swaps that with the one it holds. Neither ever waits for the other, and the bitmap's copy is the same as before the process existed
the end of the other sidethe doorbell: on Windows an event and the other process's handle, on Linux a socket pair, whose end is the end of the stream
sectionsmade by the browser. Windows: a handle duplicated into the child, with rights to map it only. Linux: a sealed memfd (a child that could shrink it would make the browser fault on a copy), its descriptor passed over a second socket

When it goes wrong. A process that ends, a process that breaks the protocol, a context with work to do that does nothing for webgl.gpu_hang_ms (twice that on a software adapter: FXC is slow there, and one hung context costs them all) or a ring nobody takes from: the process is killed, every context of the browser gets webglcontextlost, and a page that prevented its default gets webglcontextrestored once a new process has given it a device. A question keeps its deadline (webgl.wait_ms): the context that does not answer is lost at once, and the watcher kills the process if its thread does not come back; no thread is left behind. More than webgl.gpu_max_restarts bad ends within webgl.gpu_restart_window_s: getContext gives null and contexts stay lost, until that time has passed. A crash there writes no crash report of Wren's (the handler is installed by the browser's main, which the process never reaches): the page's console says how it ended, with the exit code.

It ends with its parent, even a killed one. Windows: a Job object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE named at the process's creation (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST, so that no moment exists when a child is outside it; started suspended and assigned afterwards, a parent killed in between left suspended orphans), and the child watches the parent's handle too. Linux: PR_SET_PDEATHSIG set by a thread that lives as long as the child (the signal follows the thread, not the process), and the socket's end.

What the child gives up, before any driver is loaded (webgl.gpu_keep_rights keeps it all, for a driver that needs it):

DoneNot done, and why
WindowsLow integrity (no writing to what the user's programs own, no opening their processes; a driver's shader cache under the user's profile is not written); every privilege removed; a job that allows no other process, no clipboard, no desktops, no display settings, no global atoms, no handles of other processes' windows; no extension points (AppInit DLLs, hooks); no images from the network or of Low label; no DLL search in the working directory, which is the program's own folder; only the handles it needs are inherited; no error dialogsAn AppContainer or a restricted token (a driver opens registry keys, files and kernel objects no list here could name); Win32k lockdown and no dynamic code (drivers need GDI, and compile shaders to machine code); the network
LinuxPR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS; no core dumps; every descriptor closed but its ownseccomp, namespaces, Landlock (drivers open /dev/dri and /sys, read caches, call ioctls no list here could name); the network. The environment stays, for what drivers read from it

Nothing that crosses is believed. The child ends on an unknown kind, a length past its kind's limit or an index that cannot be true; refuses attributes that cannot be; ignores contexts it does not know; the commands themselves are checked word by word (Ctx::exec). The browser kills it for the same, for a context or a question that was never asked, a count of finished work that does not add up, rows of pixels that do not fit or overflow, a frame larger than its section or a slot that does not exist; an answer larger than the asker's buffer is not kept, so that a length costs the browser no memory the page did not offer. Everything in shared memory is copied out before it is looked at.

The cost, measured on examples/site/webgl.html and examples/site/webgl-stress.html with wrentool bench webgl (the same pages, before and after, alternating, the best of the runs):

beforeafter
webgl.html, frames a second6060
stress page (5000 draws a frame, 1920 x 1080), frames a second17.517.9
its script's time per frame40 ms36 ms
the browser's first context (the process starts with it)249 ms264 ms
a later context133 ms112 ms
getError (a round trip)23 us21 us
readPixels, one pixel0.16 ms0.18 ms
readPixels, 8 MB8.2 ms9.8 ms
texImage2D, 4096 x 4096 (64 MB), with finish54 ms48 ms
bufferData, 64 MB, with finish41 ms47 ms
working set on webgl.html (browser + process)465 MB187 + 334 MB
on the stress page727 MB407 + 482 MB
a page without WebGLno processsince round 60, by default: a process with one device, made ahead at the first paint, once a browser's life when nobody uses it (webgl.gpu_start_ahead)

On a machine (RTX 4070 SUPER, 16 logical processors) that other jobs were using: differences of a few percent mean nothing here. What can be told: frames cost the same, since a frame takes the same copies; large messages pay one copy more through a ring; the memory grows by what a second process has (its copy of the runtime's data and of the drivers' loaded state, its rings, a canvas's three pictures: about 55 MB on webgl.html, 160 MB on the stress page, of which the shared memory is counted on both sides).

#Workers

OffscreenCanvas.getContext("webgl") and ("webgl2") work in a worker as in a window, their interfaces evaluated when first read there. What a page has with a context, a worker has: questions, shaders, lost and restored. requestAnimationFrame is the worker's 60 Hz clock.

  • transferToImageBitmap() asks for the drawing buffer (it waits, as readPixels does) and the frame ends: the buffer starts again as after a present.
  • An OffscreenCanvas no element shows makes no frames by itself: its pixels are fetched when it is read (convertToBlob, transferToImageBitmap, drawImage).
  • canvas.transferControlToOffscreen() makes the element a placeholder, and the OffscreenCanvas transferable in a message (Canvas_Placeholder, src/page/canvas_offscreen.odin). What it draws, WebGL or 2D, is copied at the end of each turn of its thread's loop into the placeholder, and from there into the element's bitmap by the page's thread: from a section to the worker's bitmap, then the placeholder, then the element's bitmap. Two copies more than a canvas of the page, one of them on the worker's thread (below 2 ms each for 2 megapixels).
  • Not done: the layout of a placeholder keeps following its width and height attributes, not the size the worker chooses (the picture is scaled to fit), and setting those on a placeholder does not throw. ImageBitmap is still not transferable in a message.

#Limits

  • Transform feedback: needs vertex shaders that write to storage (VERTEX_WRITABLE_STORAGE, everywhere Direct3D 12 and Vulkan have it). An adapter without it says MAX_TRANSFORM_FEEDBACK_* are 0, and beginTransformFeedback is INVALID_OPERATION. A vertex of the capture runs in a pass of its own: a program's vertex stage runs twice when it is also drawn. Strips, fans and loops copy their primitives vertex by vertex, which is slow for many.
  • Queries: no timers (EXT_disjoint_timer_query). ANY_SAMPLES_PASSED_CONSERVATIVE is ANY_SAMPLES_PASSED.
  • Compressed textures: S3TC only (WEBGL_compressed_texture_s3tc), 2D, where the adapter has BC formats. No ETC, ASTC, RGTC, BPTC.
  • Rendering: lines are 1 pixel wide. A vertex attribute divisor above 1 is written out, per instance, on each draw count. Points cannot be instanced. SAMPLE_COVERAGE is ignored. A framebuffer's depth and stencil must be one attachment. Depth blits are whole copies of the same size and samples.
  • Videos are textures when their picture is on the CPU (software decoding); a picture only on the GPU uploads nothing.
  • gl.getError from a Wasm module of a page: as JavaScript's; a malformed stream loses the context.
  • Objects collected: buffers, textures and programs a page drops without deleting stay until the page or the context goes.

#Security

Shaders and draws come from any page.

  • drawArrays and drawElements check every attribute against its buffer, and every index against the vertices (a scan, kept per range until the buffer changes): out of range is INVALID_OPERATION, never a read. wgpu checks the same on its side, and zeroes buffers and textures on creation.
  • Sizes and counts are limited: canvas.max_dimension, webgl.max_mb per context, webgl.max_contexts per page.
  • A cross-origin image or a tainted canvas in texImage2D throws SecurityError.
  • WEBGL_debug_renderer_info is left out; RENDERER says Wren WebGL.
  • The translator bounds the source (2 MiB), the tokens after macro expansion, nesting, operators per statement, else per function and the size of types: naga recurses, and its thread has a stack of 256 MiB. Each of these limits has a hostile test (a_hostile_shader_is_an_error_in_the_log). A panic in naga or wgpu loses the context; a question that gets no answer in webgl.wait_ms (10 s) loses it too.
  • A driver's own bugs, a crash inside a driver or FXC: they end the GPU process, and every context of the browser is lost (the GPU process). A page that can crash a driver can do so again, and costs other pages their contexts each time, up to webgl.gpu_max_restarts. Windows' TDR turns a shader that hangs the GPU into a device lost. Software adapters have no such thing: their contexts lose out at the deadline, and the process is killed when the thread has not come back at twice webgl.gpu_hang_ms.
  • What the GPU process can reach if a driver is compromised through a shader is what the table above leaves it: on both systems it can read what the user can and use the network.

Microsoft's software rasterizer (WARP) crashes when several devices of a process work at once (seen here): software contexts take turns, in the GPU process.

A page's thread that waits for an answer is still running its script: javascript.slow_script_ms counts the wait. On a software adapter, where FXC compiles every pipeline, a page that asks right after a burst of new programs can reach that limit under load.

#Preferences

webgl.enabled, webgl.webgl2, webgl.allow_software, webgl.force_software, webgl.backend (auto, dx12, vulkan), webgl.max_contexts, webgl.max_mb, webgl.wait_ms, webgl.gpu_hang_ms, webgl.gpu_max_restarts, webgl.gpu_restart_window_s, webgl.gpu_idle_exit_s, webgl.gpu_keep_rights, webgl.gpu_start_ahead (the tests' browsers have it off unless they ask).

#Tests

  • cargo test -p wren_webgl: the translator, formats, and a context through the C ABI on the software adapter. They pass with WREN_WEBGL_TEST_GPU=1 on a real GPU too. A machine with no adapter skips them. src/ipc_tests.rs: the channel on its own; a real child killed while drawing, hung, stalled, made hostile in each way the browser checks for, fed malformed commands and broken streams; its parent killed; the limit on restarts. A test binary is its own child (gpu_child_entry); a hook is accepted only by a child started with hooks, which a browser never asks for.
  • the web test jsweb_webgl_api (examples/jsweb/webgl.js): the interfaces and their rules on the software adapter; contexts in workers and transferControlToOffscreen. A machine with no adapter checks that getContext gives null.
  • src/tools/e2e/webgl_process.odin (in test_all): the process's life in the real browser, on the machine's GPU: its id is a number of api.Stats, and it is killed and suspended from outside under a page, its contexts and a worker's. wrentool smoke does the same under xvfb on Linux.
  • wrentool bench webgl: what WebGL costs on this machine (opt-in, not a test).
  • Demos: examples/site/webgl.html and webgl-stress.html, in about:demos.
